titulo.texto: Mural “Indigenous Peoples of Oaxaca,” by Arturo García Bustos

frase_gancho.texto: A painter who taught in Oaxaca portrayed its peoples on a wall.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the mural of the seven regions we move on to another, one of faith. Look for a painting of people walking together in a procession, the work of another student of Frida Kahlo.

guion_corto.texto: This mural was painted in 1964 by Arturo García Bustos, a painter and printmaker born in Mexico City in 1926. It was made for the Oaxaca ethnography hall, when the museum was about to open. It is a fresco, that is, a painting on wet lime. It is known both by its original title, “Indigenous Peoples of Oaxaca,” and as “Inhabitants of the Seven Regions of Oaxaca.” García Bustos learned printmaking at the Popular Graphic Workshop and was one of the four “Fridos,” the students of Frida Kahlo. In 1956 he moved to Oaxaca. His mural brings together on a single wall the people of the state, with their festivals and their trade.

guion_largo.texto:
This mural has at least three names. In 1964 it was titled “Indigenous Peoples of Oaxaca.” Other texts speak of “Inhabitants of the Seven Regions of Oaxaca.” A magazine from the INAH cites it as “Commerce, Festivals, and Tradition in the Seven Regions of Oaxaca.” All of them place it in 1964, in the Oaxaca Hall. It is probably the same work. And the three titles say something similar: people, festivals, and markets from an entire state.

It was painted by Arturo García Bustos, born in Mexico City on August 8, 1926. He died in 2017. In 1945 he joined the Popular Graphic Workshop. There he learned printmaking and lithography with Leopoldo Méndez and with Pablo O’Higgins, the painter of the wedding you saw in the Purépecha hall.

He was also one of the four “Fridos.” That was the name given to the young students whom Frida Kahlo gathered at her home in Coyoacán. The nickname plays on the name of their teacher. Another of them was Arturo Estrada, who painted the second mural in this hall, the one you will see next. A curious fact: neither of the two was born in Oaxaca. [Rufino Tamayo](mna_s00_mural_tamayo), the artist of the entrance mural, was.

In 1956 García Bustos moved to Oaxaca with his wife, the painter Rina Lazo. She is the same Rina Lazo who copied the Bonampak murals you saw in the Maya hall. He taught at the Benito Juárez University and helped revive its printmaking workshop. For him, Oaxaca was not a passing subject. It was a place where he had lived and taught.

It is painted in fresco. A fresco is painted on a layer of lime that is still wet, and as it dries the color becomes bound to the wall. That is why it is painted in sections: each day only the part to be painted is prepared. A mistake cannot be erased easily. It is the technique of the [Tepantitla mural](mna_s04_mural_tepantitla) that you saw in the Teotihuacán Hall, although that one is a modern copy.

The titles speak of seven regions. In this hall you have already toured four faces of the state. The Isthmus with the woman of Tehuantepec, the Mixtec region with the [Triqui huipil](mna_s17_huipil_triqui), the Central Valleys with the black clay, and the Coast with the Diablos. The mural joins them, and the other three, on a single wall, like a map made of people.

García Bustos painted Oaxaca again in the Government Palace of the state capital. He worked there from the late 1970s until 1987, on a series about the history, myth, and cosmogony of the Indigenous peoples. In 2026 it was one hundred years since his birth, and Oaxaca paid him tribute.

Before moving on, run your eyes slowly over the mural, the way you read a map. Look for the clothing, the busy hands, the gestures of celebration. Each painted face represents a people, and Oaxaca has so many that no single painting can exhaust them.

texto: Look for the costumes: how many different peoples do you think you can recognize?
Compare the painted clothing with the Triqui huipil and the dress of a Tehuantepec woman that you have already seen
See whether there are market or festival scenes, as one of its titles suggests

texto.Author: Arturo García Bustos (1926-2017)
texto.Work: “Indigenous Peoples of Oaxaca,” also cited as “Inhabitants of the Seven Regions of Oaxaca”

texto.pregunta: Myth: Only Zapotec and Mixtec people live in Oaxaca.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Oaxaca is the state with the most peoples and languages in the country, and that is why this mural brings together the people of seven regions and not of just one.
